3.0.0.en: “1 And he shewed me Joshua the high priest standing before the angel of the LORD, and Satan standing at his right hand to resist him. 2 And the LORD said unto Satan, ‘The LORD rebuke thee, O Satan; even the LORD that hath chosen Jerusalem rebuke thee: is not this a brand plucked out of the fire?’” [1-2].

3.0.1.en: What does this vision mean? The high priest was a symbol of the service of the temple, and by his captivity in Babylon the destruction of all the service of the temple appeared. But behind this lies a hidden enmity, not between Babylon and the high priest, but between the devil and God. Satan stood at the right hand of Joshua to resist him, but Joshua understands that the war is against God Himself, therefore he said: “The LORD rebuke thee.”

3.0.2.en: “The LORD that hath chosen Jerusalem rebuke thee”: not because of any merit on her part or any righteousness in her of herself, nor because she met the bitterness of captivity, but because God in His love chose her. As the Lord Christ assured His disciples: “Ye have not chosen me, but I have chosen you, and ordained you” (Jn 15:16). He is zealous over us because of His love for us, especially as He sees Satan as “a brand plucked out of the fire,” whose work is to cast himself into us to make of us a furnace that is never quenched.

3.0.3.en: Who is Joshua the son of Jehozadak the great priest? The Fathers see in Joshua a type of Jesus Christ, the Great High Priest and Bishop of our souls. For the word “Jesus” is shortened from Joshua, that is, “Jeho-salvation,” while “Jehozadak” means “God is righteousness.” Our Lord Jesus came to us as God our Savior and our righteousness; He came bearing our nature, so Satan did not perceive His true identity but doubted about Him, especially as He hungered and thirsted and suffered... So he stood at His right hand to resist Him, and the Lord overcame him and triumphed over him on our behalf.

3.0.4.en: The Lord Christ fought Satan, who is “a brand plucked out of the fire,” the destructive brand that men chose for themselves, which inflamed them with the fire of deadly passions. As St. Clement of Alexandria says: [Why do men flee to this deadly brand and die by it, when it is possible for them to live honored in God?!]. St. Didymus the Blind sees that Satan is a brand plucked out of the fire, which God could have left to burn without plucking it out, but He did not allow him to be punished with the full punishment for the present; rather He plucked him out to use him for His divine purposes, without Satan bearing fruit, like a branch struck by the fire to which life does not return. The Lord uses him as an instrument in which He is glorified by the victory of His children over him.

3.1.0.en: 3 Now Joshua was clothed with filthy garments, and stood before the angel. 4 And he answered and spake unto those that stood before him, saying, Take away the filthy garments from him. And unto him he said, Behold, I have caused thine iniquity to pass from thee, and I will clothe thee with change of raiment. 5 And I said, Let them set a fair mitre upon his head. So they set a fair mitre upon his head, and clothed him with garments. And the angel of the LORD stood by.

3.1.1.en: We should not wonder that Joshua appeared clothed in filthy garments and standing before the angel to hear the command issued: Take away the filthy garments from him, for Joshua is a type of Jesus Christ, the incarnate Word of God, who bore our filthy garments so that by His Cross our sins might be taken away from us, that we might bear His righteousness and be crowned.

3.1.2.en: St. Jerome says: [The Lord bore these garments, and so He gave the enemy the opportunity to stand before Him to resist Him; since He put on our sins, in this he is His adversary].

3.1.3.en: St. Didymus the Blind says: [After they took away the filthy garments from him they put the fair mitre on his head and clothed him with garments. For the sake of the re-establishment of the city and the temple and their building, the chief of the captives who were set free puts on the garments of salvation and the robe of righteousness, saying: “My soul shall be joyful in my God; for he hath clothed me with the garments of salvation, he hath covered me with the robe of righteousness” (Isa 61:10). The filthy garments are cast off from him, since he must no longer grieve but rejoice and exult in the salvation of those who endured captivity. But who are those to whom the command was given to take off from him the garments of sorrow, which were described as filthy..? It may be said that they are the angels who surround those who fear God, protect them, and keep them from feeling the anxiety and sorrow which the trials of life bring].

3.1.4.en: It was said to Joshua: “I have caused thine iniquity to pass from thee, and I will clothe thee with change of raiment” [3-4].

3.1.5.en: How is it said to him: “I have caused thine iniquity to pass from thee”? Our teacher Paul the Apostle says: “For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him” (2 Cor 5:21); “Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us: for it is written, Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree: that the blessing of Abraham might come on the Gentiles through Jesus Christ; that we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith” (Gal 3:13-14). It is as though He bore what was ours of sins so that by the Cross He might remove them and we might bear His righteousness.

3.1.6.en: As for the adorned garment that the Lord put on in place of the filthy garments, it signifies His Church adorned with manifold gifts, like the coat of many colors that Jacob gave to his son Joseph. Each one of us represents a thread in this garment; if it is pulled out, the garment loses its beauty and its strength. This is the garment in which the Lord is transfigured and becomes radiant as the light (Mt 17:2). As St. Augustine says: [His garments are the Church, for if the one who wears them does not hold them, they fall; in this garment Paul was as a hem, since he said of himself: “For I am the least of the apostles” (1 Cor 15:9)... Therefore the woman who suffered from an issue of blood, when she touched the hem of the garment of the Lord Christ, was healed. So the Church that came from the Gentiles became whole through the teachings of Paul the Apostle].

3.1.7.en: St. Gregory of Nyssa sees that the putting off of the filthy garments and the putting on of the adorned garment signifies putting off our old man and our enjoyment of the new man through the waters of Baptism, as he says: [By this we learn in a symbolic way that in the baptism of the Lord Christ we put off our sins like a poor and filthy garment and put on the holy garment of renewal, which is most fitting].

3.1.8.en: As for the fair mitre, it is the crown with which we are crowned in the holy Lord.

3.2.s.en: 3. Joshua, the worker in the house of the Lord:

3.2.0.en: 6 And the angel of the LORD protested unto Joshua, saying, 7 “Thus saith the LORD of hosts; If thou wilt walk in my ways, and if thou wilt keep my charge, then thou shalt also judge my house, and shalt also keep my courts, and I will give thee places to walk among these that stand by. 8 Hear now, O Joshua the high priest, thou, and thy fellows that sit before thee: for they are men wondered at: for, behold, I will bring forth my servant the BRANCH. 9 For behold the stone that I have laid before Joshua; upon one stone shall be seven eyes: behold, I will engrave the graving thereof, saith the LORD of hosts, and I will remove the iniquity of that land in one day. 10 In that day, saith the LORD of hosts, shall ye call every man his neighbour under the vine and under the fig tree.”

3.3.0.en: The commandment presented to us has become directed to our Head and Great High Priest, Jesus Christ: “Thus saith the LORD of hosts; If thou wilt walk in my ways, and if thou wilt keep my charge, then thou shalt also judge my house, and shalt also keep my courts, and I will give thee places to walk among these that stand by” [7]. The secret of presenting the commandment to Him is that we cannot carry it out except through Him, and we cannot fulfil the charges of God without His work in us.

3.3.1.en: If the Church is the house of God, then our Lord Jesus is the One who judges the Church, upholding those who stand and raising the fallen; thus His children are “standing,” that is, risen in Him, and He finds for Himself a way to walk among them.

3.3.2.en: Finally He concludes this vision by revealing the person of this great priest: “For, behold, I will bring forth my servant the Branch, the East is his name: for behold the stone that I have laid before Joshua; upon one stone shall be seven eyes: behold, I will engrave the graving thereof, saith the LORD of hosts, shall ye call every man his neighbour under the vine and under the fig tree” [8-15].

3.3.3.en: We can summarize His discourse here about the person of our Lord Jesus Christ as follows:

3.3.4.en: First: He calls Him: My servant, the Branch, the East, the Stone; each title completes the rest of the titles. Through the Incarnation He became a servant, for He “made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men” (Phil 2:6-7). And by His descent from David the king He came forth as a branch, though He is the Creator of the vine (Isa 11:1-2); as for His being called the East, it is because He is the Sun of Righteousness who shines upon those sitting in darkness. And finally He was called the Stone, since the builders rejected Him and He became the chief cornerstone, joining Jews and Gentiles together in the heavenly spiritual building of which the Apostle said: “built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone” (Eph 2:20).

3.3.5.en: Second: He says: “I will remove the iniquity of that land in one day,” which is the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ as the Sun that has risen upon us without setting, turning our night into a day without night; in Him our iniquities were taken away by the Cross.

3.3.6.en: Third: In that day, the day of the Cross, we were bound together: “shall ye call every man his neighbour under the fig tree,” that is, our being bound together in Him by love through His Church, the holy vine and the fruitful fig tree. In our study of the Book of Hosea we saw how the vine signifies the suffering Church that passes through the winepress with her Bridegroom, and the fig tree the unity of the Holy Spirit, who is indicated by the fig's husk which contains within it many seeds that have no value except through the unity of the Spirit.

4.0.0.en: “And the angel that talked with me came again, and waked me, as a man that is wakened out of his sleep.” [1].

4.0.1.en: Perhaps the sleep of Zechariah the prophet reveals the distress of soul of Zerubbabel, who found resistance from outside and inside, and since the prophet Zechariah could not support him, he slept. Perhaps by this he played the same role that the disciples played in the garden, who did not endure the events from merely hearing about them, so they slept, and the Lord came to rebuke them, addressing Peter the Apostle: “Couldest not thou watch one hour? Watch ye and pray, lest ye enter into temptation” (Mk 14:37-38).

4.1.0.en: 2 And said unto me, What seest thou? And I said, I have looked, and behold a candlestick all of gold, with a bowl upon the top of it, and his seven lamps thereon, and seven pipes to the seven lamps, which are upon the top thereof: 3 And two olive trees by it, one upon the right side of the bowl, and the other upon the left side thereof. 4 So I answered and spake to the angel that talked with me, saying, What are these, my lord? 5 Then the angel that talked with me answered and said unto me, Knowest thou not what these be? And I said, No, my lord. 6 Then he answered and spake unto me, saying, This is the word of the LORD unto Zerubbabel, saying, Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts. 7 Who art thou, O great mountain? before Zerubbabel thou shalt become a plain: and he shall bring forth the corner stone amid those who cry, Honor, honor to him.

4.1.1.en: Since the house was being rebuilt by the hands of Zerubbabel, the thought of the prophet and of all the faithful in the service of the Lord soared, floating in the glory of this house and of what it contained of furnishings, especially the golden ones that the Lord commanded Moses to prepare, among them the golden lampstand with its seven lamps. In this vision God drew the heart of the prophet to see the return of the golden lampstand, which represents the illumination of the temple with the oil of divine grace and the work of the Holy Spirit. But this lampstand differed in some of its details from the traditional lampstand (Ex 37:17-24), and two olive trees surrounded it here, one on the right of the bowl of the lampstand and the other on its left.

4.2.s.en: Note the following about this lampstand:

4.2.0.en: First: The lampstand is golden, that is, heavenly and spiritual, a symbol of the Church (Rev 1:20), and it bears the heavenly character, so it needs its heavenly Bridegroom Himself as its helper and keeper. As St. Didymus the Blind says: [When he says that the lampstand is all gold [2], it shows us that the lampstand that is wholly filled with light is a spiritual, not a material, lampstand. This golden lampstand represents the dwelling of God and His temple, as it is written in the Book of Revelation: “The mystery of the seven stars which thou sawest in my right hand, and the seven golden candlesticks. The seven stars are the angels of the seven churches: and the seven candlesticks which thou sawest are the seven churches” (Rev 1:20)].

4.2.1.en: Second: He says: “a bowl upon the top of it.” It is as though this lampstand represents the Church enlightened by the Holy Spirit, which the Lord Christ likens to five wise virgins who carried oil in their vessels and went out to meet the bridegroom (Mt 25). St. Augustine sees in this oil the love of God and of one's neighbor, which the Holy Spirit pours out abundantly in us. Whoever has the love of God in him carries the divine light and enjoys the Kingdom, while whoever loses love is in darkness and cannot behold God.

4.2.2.en: Third: “and his seven lamps thereon, and seven pipes to the seven lamps, which are upon the top thereof” [2].

4.3.0.en: St. Didymus the Blind says: [As the bowl is above the lampstand, so the seven lamps appear above it, so that the light is multiplied seven times, because just as perfect luminous knowledge has been likened to seven eyes [9], and just as the seven pillars bear the dwelling of wisdom: “Wisdom hath builded her house, she hath hewn out her seven pillars” (Prov 9:1), so the lampstand bears seven lamps. And the lampstand represents the Lord the Savior since it is all gold, because the Lord “did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth” (1 Pet 2:22), and there rests upon Him like seven lamps: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of divine counsel and might, of knowledge and godliness and the fear of the Lord (Isa 11:2)].

4.3.1.en: And the Church also, since she bears the characteristics of her Bridegroom and enjoys His righteousness, becomes a golden lampstand without spot or wrinkle (Eph 5:27), her light not from herself but the light of her Bridegroom the “Sun of Righteousness,” who shines without setting, He who sent to her His Holy Spirit to enlighten her in the midst of the world. As for the seven pipes, they are the means of salvation through which the Holy Spirit works in the Church, especially the seven Sacraments. This is the essence of the vision: the confirmation of the work of the Holy Spirit in the Church, as He says: “Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts. Who art thou, O great mountain? before Zerubbabel thou shalt become a plain” [6-7].

4.3.2.en: From the historical side, the resistance against Zerubbabel was like a great mountain that no human arm could move, until Zerubbabel doubted the completion of the work, but the Lord assured him that He Himself would complete the work [8]. God turned this great mountain before him into a plain. From the spiritual side, the disciples also needed the Holy Spirit so that the great mountain of preaching might become a plain, for the Lord said to them: “But ye shall receive power, after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you: and ye shall be witnesses unto me both in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea, and in Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth” (Acts 1:4-8).

4.3.3.en: If we may say that the preaching of the Crucified among the Jews was a stumblingblock and foolishness (1 Cor 1:23), as though it were a great mountain, then by the Holy Spirit this mountain became a plain before the Apostles and disciples. Therefore the Lord continues His speech: “and he shall bring forth the corner stone amid those who cry, Honor, honor to him” [7]. It is as though the work of the Holy Spirit in them is the witness to the Lord Christ, the cornerstone who bound Jews and Gentiles together in Himself, and all cry out, “Honor, honor to him.” As for the repetition of the word “honor,” it signifies the people who are of two origins, Jewish and Gentile, and it also signifies the nature of love that belongs to the new people, for St. Augustine sees that the number 2 signifies love, so no one can witness to the Crucified and glorify Him unless he bears in him this loving nature.

4.3.4.en: St. Didymus the Blind says: [Apart from the interpretation we presented, there is another view which says that the mountain symbolizes the Virgin Mary, and the stone coming out of it symbolizes Christ whom she bore without marriage, and the prophet Daniel teaches us these mysteries, saying: “Thou sawest till that a stone was cut out without hands, which smote the image upon his feet that were of iron and clay, and brake them to pieces” (Dan 2:34). He says that the stone that smites the various kingdoms and the image that it formed was cut out of the mountain without the help of hands, done without the work of parents... and Christ alone is the One who was born of a virgin. Before Zerubbabel the stone was cut out of the mountain without the help of hands].

4.3.5.en: If this great mountain is the Lady the Virgin who bore the Lord Christ without the seed of man, a matter that seemed impossible yet was fulfilled, then it also signifies the soul that bears within it the Lord Christ spiritually, as St. Cyril the Great says: [Through the Spirit Christ is formed in us and stamps His features on us, and thus the beauty of His divinity becomes alive again in the nature of man].

4.3.6.en: Fourth: “And two olive trees by it, one upon the right side of the bowl, and the other upon the left side thereof” [3]. Perhaps these two olive trees signify Zerubbabel and Joshua, anointed to rebuild the temple, for they are the “sons of oil” [14]. One carries out the material role and the other the spiritual work, without duality, but each completes the other and supports him.

4.3.7.en: If the oil signifies the work of the Holy Spirit who enlightens the soul with true knowledge, then the olive tree on the right, in the view of St. Didymus, signifies the knowledge of divine things, while the second signifies the study of the world and its order and the arrangement of divine providence for it.

4.3.8.en: St. Didymus also sees that the two olive trees signify Moses and Elijah, who appeared on the right and on the left of the Lord at the moments of the Transfiguration (Lk 9:30), since the Law is spiritual, a son of anointing, and the word of prophecy is also spiritual; and the two witness to the glory of the Lord and His divinity.

4.3.9.en: Perhaps the two olive trees signify the Holy Bible with its two Testaments, for the Holy Spirit uses it to enlighten our heart with the light of knowledge and the manifestation of the Lord within us.

4.4.0.en: 8 Moreover the word of the LORD came unto me, saying, 9 The hands of Zerubbabel have laid the foundation of this house; his hands shall also finish it; and thou shalt know that the LORD of hosts hath sent me unto you. 10 For who hath despised the day of small things? Those seven shall rejoice, and shall see the plummet in the hand of Zerubbabel; they are the eyes of the LORD, which run to and fro through the whole earth. 11 Then answered I, and said unto him, What are these two olive trees upon the right side of the candlestick and upon the left side thereof? 12 And I answered again, and said unto him, What be these two olive branches which through the two golden pipes empty the golden oil out of themselves? 13 And he answered me and said, Knowest thou not what these be? And I said, No, my lord. 14 Then said he, These are the two sons of oil, that stand by the LORD of the whole earth.

4.4.1.en: This vision came to give Zerubbabel assurance regarding the following:

4.4.2.en: First: The work is not accomplished by a human arm but by the Spirit of God [6-7].

4.5.0.en: Second: God confirms the completion of the work by the hand of Zerubbabel, even if it remained suspended for years because of the resistance [9].

4.6.0.en: Third: God rejoices in the work that many despised when they compared it with the first temple, counting it [small things] [10]... In their eyes it is a small work, indeed as nothing (Hag 2:3), but God rejoices in it as His seven eyes, roving through the whole earth, look upon it, not to criticize and condemn but to rejoice in the work of the children of God and strengthen their hands (2 Chr 16:9). The eyes of the Lord see the plummet in the hand of Zerubbabel [10], that is, they see him holding the instrument that measures the straightness of the building (which was usually of lead in the form of a weight tied to a string).
